q: Most Bordeaux chateaux sell their wine through whom?
exp: The chateau sells to negociant merchants, brokered by courtiers, who distribute onward. Few great estates sell direct.

q: A chateau's junior label, made from younger vines and declassified lots, is called what?
exp: Second wines let a chateau keep the grand vin strict while still selling the rest, and they carry the house style at a lower price.

q: Red Bordeaux is traditionally matured in barrels of what size?
exp: The 225 litre barrique is the Bordeaux standard, and its surface-to-volume ratio is much of why the region's oak influence is what it is.

q: The network of negociants and courtiers that trades Bordeaux is called what?
exp: The Place is the trading system itself, and it now distributes wines from well beyond Bordeaux.

q: Left Bank and Right Bank soils differ broadly in what way?
opts: Gravel on the Left, clay on the Right
Volcanic on the Left, granite on the Right
Chalk on the Left, sand on the Right
exp: On the cotes of Saint-Emilion that clay sits over limestone, while Pomerol's lies on gravel and the iron pan, and the difference is why the grape emphasis flips across the water: gravel for late Cabernet Sauvignon, cooler clay for earlier Merlot.

q: Saint-Emilion's limestone plateau particularly suits which variety?
exp: Limestone holds moisture in reserve and keeps acidity, which suits Merlot. Cabernet Franc does well there too.

q: In Bordeaux, what does the word chateau denote?
exp: Chateau names an estate and its vineyard holdings. Many carry no building of the kind the word suggests.

q: Well-drained gravel warms readily. Which ripening problem does that help solve?
opts: Loss of colour in the skins
exp: Warmth at the root and free drainage push a late variety over the line. In wet years drainage matters as much as the heat.

q: Where does Cru Bourgeois sit relative to the 1855 growths?
opts: It is another name for Fifth Growths
exp: Cru Bourgeois is a separate Medoc ranking for estates the 1855 list did not include, and it has been reorganised several times.

q: Bordeaux Superieur differs from basic Bordeaux AOC in what respect?
opts: It must come from the Medoc
It must be a single variety
exp: Superieur is a stricter version of the regional appellation rather than a different place: a lower maximum yield, a higher minimum alcohol and a longer ageing period, with the fruit still drawn from anywhere in the region.

q: The Cote d'Or divides into which two halves?
opts: The Cote de Beaune and Beaujolais
Chablis and the Cote de Nuits
The Cote de Nuits and the Cote de Beaune
The Cote Chalonnaise and the Maconnais
exp: Nuits to the north, Beaune to the south. The Cote d'Or is a narrow escarpment barely a few hundred metres wide in places, and it carries almost every famous name.

q: Which half of the Cote d'Or is overwhelmingly planted to red wine?
exp: The Cote de Nuits is Pinot Noir country and holds most of the red Grands Crus. The Cote de Beaune makes both, and holds the great whites.

q: Chablis sits well to the north of the Cote d'Or, closer to which other region?
exp: The isolation is the point: Chablis is nearer Champagne than Beaune, and the cool northerly site is why the wines are as taut as they are.

q: Running south from the Cote d'Or, which region comes next?
exp: The order running south is Cote d'Or, Cote Chalonnaise, Maconnais, then Beaujolais. Prices tend to fall in the same direction.

q: Beaujolais lies at the southern end of Burgundy. Which grape dominates it?
exp: Gamay was expelled from the Cote d'Or in the fourteenth century and found its home on Beaujolais granite, where it makes something entirely its own.

q: Which Burgundian sub-region is the largest source of the region's Chardonnay by volume?
exp: The Maconnais produces far more white than the Cote d'Or, at prices that make Burgundian Chardonnay approachable at all.
